notes.1a: Most candidates gave the correct answers. A few lost a mark for rounding $25.56 to $26.00.
notes.1bi: Many candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to calculate the percentage that needed to be borrowed, 15%.
notes.1bii: Fewer candidates gave the correct answer. Many candidates only found the amount borrowed, $660, and then worked out the interest rather than the total amount owed. A few candidates used $4400 or $3740 instead of $660.
notes.1c: Many candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to misread the question and multiply $321 by 12 instead of dividing by 12.
notes.1d: Many candidates found this part challenging. Although many candidates correctly identified that the van would travel further they omitted to give a valid reason for their decision. In particular, some candidates made a calculation which, although correct, was evaluated to an insufficient degree of accuracy to be useful in making the final decision.
notes.1e: Although most candidates showed an understanding of ratios, many only found one part, 1400, instead of two parts, 2800. Some candidates found the amount for repairs instead of fuel. Answers: (a) 258(.00), 25.56, 758.56 (b)(i) 85 (ii) 739.2(0) (c) 26.75 (d) Van and 12.6 > 12.4 (e) 2800
notes.2ai: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to give an answer of 24.30 – 23.85 rather than evaluating it. A few candidates gave a range for the distance rather than the time.
notes.2aii: Candidates generally gave the correct answer. Again, some candidates used the wrong data, time instead of distance.
notes.2bi: Most candidates showed an understanding of how to plot points with many correctly plotting the required points with good accuracy. The most common error was to misread the scale on the x -axis and plot all the points between 24.0 and 24.1.
notes.2bii: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates embellished their answers with words such as weak or strong. A small number of candidates omitted to give an answer.
notes.2biii: A large number of candidates thought that the given statement was correct. Many candidates who did say that the statement was not correct gave a good explanation.
notes.2biv: Although many candidates drew a reasonable line of best fit a similar number of candidates did not. The most common errors were to join up every point or simply join the first point to the last point. A few candidates attempted to fit a positive line to the data.
notes.2bv: Most candidates showed that they understood how to read from a line of best fit. Occasionally the scale on the y -axis was misread. Answers: (a)(i) [0].45 (ii) 6.115 or 6.12 (b)(ii) Negative
notes.3ai: Many correct answers were given by the candidates.
notes.3aii: Many correct answers were given by the candidates. The most common error was to give an answer of 71.
notes.3b: Few candidates scored 3 marks; many candidates scored 2 marks for 43. Many candidates did not give suitable reasons for their answer with most simply showing the calculation they performed rather than stating the geometrical properties behind the calculation. Where candidates did state the properties, some candidates lost the last mark as they only mentioned angles in a triangle and omitted angles on a straight line.
notes.3c: About half the candidates calculated the correct answer. Some candidates tried using the cosine rule or Pythagoras’ theorem but invariably didn’t give a complete method.
notes.3di: This part was well answered by many candidates. The main error was to find 375 and assume that this had proved the result.
notes.3dii: Candidates found this part challenging. Most candidates divided 375 by 450 but many inverted these numbers. Some candidates added their answer directly to 14 45 not recognising that their number was in hours rather than minutes. Quite a few candidates used 100 minutes in an hour especially when their first part answer was 1.2. A few candidates did not use the 24-hour clock. Answers: (a)(i) 35 (ii) 74 (b) 43 (c) 32.2 (d)(ii) 15 35
notes.4ai: Many candidates made good attempts at the construction. The most common errors were for either the line AB to not be vertical or to not show the construction arcs.
notes.4aii: Some candidates gave the correct bearing. The most common error was to find the bearing of A from C rather than C from A .
notes.4aiii: Quite a few candidates did not answer this part. Many gave an answer of 360 − 23 rather than 180+23.
notes.4b: Very few candidates gained full marks for this part. Most candidates understood they needed to construct a large arc of 6 cm around the point W . Very few candidates drew this arc inaccurately. Most candidates then drew arcs of similar length from P and T and marked their intersections with the original arc as the possible positions for the ship. Very few candidates attempted to construct a perpendicular bisector between P and T and those that did generally gained full marks. Answers: (a)(ii) [0]37 to [0]41 (iii) 203
notes.5ai: Many candidates gave the correct answers. A few candidates misread the question and wrote 8 and 9 rather than 64 and 81. A few candidates just wrote 8 and 9.
notes.5aii: Candidates tended to misunderstand this question. Although a large minority of candidates gave a correct answer of 90 and a few candidates gave an alternative correct answer of 1350, many candidates found a common factor, either 3 or 5. A substantial number of candidates did not give an answer to this part.
notes.5aiii: Many candidates showed an understanding of factors. Some candidates gave the correct answer. The most common errors were to either misread the question and include the even factors as well or only give three of the factors, with normally 1 or 27 being missed.
notes.5aiv: The majority of candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to give the common factors rather than the highest common factor.
notes.5b: Candidates made a good attempt at this question with a small majority gaining full marks. The most 2 5 common omission was to not show the division by as a multiplication by . Another omission 5 2 which was not so common was to misread the question and not turn their answer into a mixed number.
notes.5ci: Nearly all candidates gave the correct answer. The majority of candidates stated the rule as “add 3” but some candidates wrote the n th term, 3 n + 5. Others gave the n th term as n + 3.
notes.5cii: Slightly fewer candidates gave the correct answer here. Again the common error was in the rule with n − 8 being frequently stated although some candidates did give 33 − 8 n .
notes.5civ: Most candidates found this part challenging. Many candidates tried to find a difference between terms. A few candidates did give a correct next term but could not give a rule. Answers: (a)(i) 64, 81 (ii) 90 k (iii) 1, 3, 9, 27 (iv) 16 (b) (c)(i) 20, add 3 (ii) –7, subtract 8
notes.6a: Many candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to assume that a hexagon had a different number of sides with 8 h being seen frequently. Another fairly common error was to multiply the sides together instead of adding them so h was sometimes seen.
notes.6bi: Slightly more candidates gave the correct answer. The most common error was to multiply the sides together instead of adding them, usually when the same error had been made in the previous part.
notes.6bii: Many candidates gave the correct answer. However, a substantial number of candidates did not recognise that this part was related to the previous part with sides equal to x and just wrote down length x breadth.
notes.6c: Some candidates found this part challenging with a substantial number not giving an answer. Of those candidates that attempted this part, many did not write down the correct expression for the perimeter but subsequently did equate this to 53 and solved their expression correctly and scored some part marks. Those candidates who only wrote down a final incorrect answer could not score any part marks.
notes.6d: The clear majority of candidates gave the correct answer. The most frequent error was to mishandle the negative signs with answers such as 6 a − b being seen frequently.
notes.6ei: Nearly all candidates gave the correct answer. The few who gave an incorrect answer tended to omit multiplying the second term inside the bracket by 5 so 5 x − 4 was commonly seen here.
notes.6eii: Slightly fewer candidates gave the correct answer. Those candidates who incorrectly multiplied out the expression in the previous part tended to make the same error here. A few candidates tried to simplify the expression further by giving the final answer as either 4x or 4x .
notes.6f: Only a minority of candidates gave the fully factorised answer. The majority of candidates gave partially factorised answers such as 2 x (4 x − 2) or x (8 x − 4). A few candidates mishandled the 2 2 factorisation, giving answers such as 4 x arising from incorrectly taking x out of the expression to give x (8 − 4). 2 3 Answers: (a) 6 h (b)(i) 4 x (ii) x (c) 7.5 (d) 6 a + b (e)(i) 5 x – 20 (ii) x + 3 x (f) 4 x (2 x – 1)

notes.7d: Many candidates recognised this as an enlargement and slightly more gave the other two requirements to describe the transformation correctly. notes.8a: The majority of candidates gave the correct answers. The main error was when evaluating the values for x = − 3 and x = − 2 where the negative sign was often not used correctly.
notes.8b: Most candidates plotted their points correctly. There was little evidence of joining points with straight lines.
notes.8c: Many candidates knew where to draw the line y = 6.
notes.8d: Many candidates gave correct answers for their curve. The common error was to not recognise that each small square on the two axes had different values, 0.2 on the x -axis and 0.4 on the y -axis. Answers: (a) 15, 8, 0, 0, 8 (d) − 1.8 or –1.7 or –1.6, 3.6 or 3.7 or 3.8
notes.9a: Generally, candidates gave the correct answer. Some candidates did not recognise that they needed to obtain the factor in order to complete this part.
